theme.toggle: Switch between light and dark colours

dialog.resetBody: This clears the canvas. All elements and wires will be removed.
dialog.switchBody: This clears the canvas so you can start fresh at the new level.

file.menuHint: Save your chain, open one, or share it
file.saveBody: Your chain is saved as a file (usually in your Downloads folder). Open it again later with File → Open.
file.pictureTitle: Save a picture of your chain
file.pictureBody: A PNG picture of everything on the canvas — for a worksheet or a chat. The chain is hidden inside the picture too: File → Open turns it back into the chain.
file.openBody: There are already elements on the canvas. Replace them with this chain, or add it beside them?
file.levelReplace: It was made at the {level} level: replacing the canvas switches the app to {level}.
file.levelAdd: It was made at the {level} level, so the app switches to {level}.
file.skipped: {count} elements were left out: this version of the app does not have them.
file.linkCopied: Link copied. Anyone who opens it gets a copy of this chain.
file.linkLong: Link copied — but it is very long, so some chat apps may cut it short. Saving a file is safer.
file.linkFailed: The link could not be copied. Save the chain to a file instead.
file.linkBroken: This link is broken or cut short, so the chain could not be opened. Ask for the link again.
file.pictureSaved: Picture saved — usually in your Downloads folder.
file.pictureFailed: The picture could not be made. Try again, or save a file instead.
file.notChain: This file isn't a saved signal chain. Open a .json file or a picture saved from this app.
file.noChainInPicture: This picture has no chain inside. Only pictures saved from this app can be opened.

toolbar.snapHint: Line elements up on the dotted grid

tools.label: What a click does
tools.dragHint: Drag an element to move it. Drag empty space to look around the canvas.
tools.selectHint: Click elements to pick several (click again to drop one), or drag a box around them. Then right-click one to copy or duplicate them all.
tools.removeHint: Click an element or a wire to remove it.
tools.redoHint: Bring back the change you just took back.

connecting.hint: Click a highlighted input. Click empty space to add a bend.

beginner.title: Beginner
beginner.description: Simple chain: microphone → preamp → EQ → compressor → speaker.

intermediate.title: Intermediate
intermediate.description: Full chain including channel fader and master bus.

advanced.title: Advanced
advanced.description: Full chain with all processing stages.

warnings.domainMixedBus: Cannot mix analog and digital signals — insert a DAC before this bus, or keep signals in the same domain.
warnings.digitalToAmp: Amp cannot amplify a digital signal. Insert a DAC before the amp to convert back to analog.
warnings.digitalToSpeaker: Speaker cannot receive a digital signal. Insert a DAC before the speaker.
warnings.adcExpectsAnalog: ADC expects an analog input. Connect it after analog gear, not after another ADC or digital node.
warnings.dacExpectsDigital: DAC expects a digital input. Connect it after an ADC or other digital node.

eq.label: Parametric Equalizer
eq.widthShelf: A shelf has no width — turn Shelf off to use it
eq.shelfHint: Shelf: raise or lower everything past this frequency evenly, instead of a hump around it
eq.graphHint: Drag a coloured dot up to make that range louder, down to make it quieter, or sideways to move it to lower or higher sounds. Double-click a dot to set it back to 0 dB (no change).
eq.graphHintWidth: Scroll over a dot to make its band wider or narrower.

graphic-eq.label: Graphic EQ
graphic-eq.hint: Drag a slider up to boost that frequency, down to cut it. Double-click = 0 dB.
graphic-eq.flatHint: Set every slider back to 0 dB

speaker.needsAmp: Silent — needs an Amplifier before it

active-speaker.label: Active Speaker

mic.what: The microphone converts sound (acoustic energy) into an electrical signal. It outputs a very weak voltage — typically around -60 dBu for a dynamic microphone.
mic.why: Everything starts here. The quality and placement of the microphone determines the raw material for the entire signal chain. A good source signal makes everything downstream easier.
mic.tip: The signal is in the blue (too quiet) zone — that is completely normal and expected at this stage. The preamp's job is to fix that.

line-in.what: A line input accepts signals that are already at "line level" — roughly -10 dBu for consumer gear, +4 dBu for professional gear. This is the standard level used between devices: from a keyboard, audio interface, or effects unit into a mixer.
line-in.why: Line-level signals are strong enough to drive mixing and processing gear directly without a preamp. They sit well above the noise floor and well below the clipping point.
line-in.tip: If your line-level signal looks green (-40 to 0 dBu) you are good to go. If it is too quiet, the source device may have its own output level control — adjust that first before adding gain in the chain. Set it to Stereo for a source that has a left and a right side, like a keyboard or a phone — both travel on one wire.

instrument.what: An instrument input (also called "Hi-Z" or high impedance) is designed for direct connection of guitars, basses, and similar passive pickups. The signal is louder than a microphone but still below true line level — typically -30 to -10 dBu.
instrument.why: Guitar pickups have a high output impedance. Connecting them to a standard line input or mic input causes tone loss (the high frequencies get loaded down). An instrument input has the correct impedance — 1 MΩ or more — to let the signal pass without colouring it.
instrument.tip: Going direct (DI) from an instrument bypasses the amp entirely. This is common in recording and live sound. A DI box can also be used to convert the high-impedance signal to a low-impedance balanced mic-level signal, which travels well over long cables.

gain.what: A gain stage turns a signal up or down by a set amount: right of 0 dB makes it louder, left of 0 dB quieter, and all the way left switches it off. Placed right after a microphone, this same card becomes a Preamp.
gain.why: Every device in a chain expects a certain level. A gain stage fixes a signal that arrives too weak or too strong — a quiet line source, say, or a hot one before an effect that would clip.
gain.tip: Start at 0 dB (no change) and move it only until the meter after it sits in the green (−40 to 0 dBu). Turning up raises the noise along with the signal; turning down too far leaves the next stage too little to work with.

preamp.what: The preamplifier (preamp) boosts the weak microphone-level signal up to "line level" — strong enough for the rest of the chain to work with. Typical gain: +20 to +60 dB. It is what the Gain card becomes when you place it right after a microphone.
preamp.why: Without enough gain here, all downstream processors — EQ, compressor, fader — work with a weak signal and introduce more noise. Too much gain causes distortion before anything else can help.
preamp.tip: Aim for the output to land in the green zone (-40 to 0 dBu). This is called gain staging, and it starts right here at the preamp.

hpf.what: The High-Pass Filter (HPF) removes frequencies below a chosen cutoff point. Everything below that frequency is rolled off — "blocked". Everything above it "passes" through unchanged.
hpf.why: Microphones and instruments pick up low-frequency rumble: air conditioning, footsteps, handling noise, mic stand vibration. These frequencies serve no musical purpose and just muddy the mix. The HPF cleans them up before they reach the EQ or compressor.
hpf.tip: For most vocals start at 80–120 Hz. For acoustic guitar, try 100–150 Hz. Never use HPF on a kick drum or bass — you'll cut the fundamental frequency you actually want. The curve display shows exactly which frequencies you're removing.

eq.what: The equalizer (EQ) shapes the tonal character of the signal by boosting or cutting frequency ranges. Each band targets a frequency area: Low (body), Mid (presence), High (air and clarity). A Bell band makes a peak or dip around its frequency; a Shelf band boosts or cuts everything below or above it, evenly.
eq.why: Every sound source has frequencies that help or hurt its purpose. A vocal may need less boxiness around 400 Hz, more presence at 3 kHz, and more air at 10 kHz. The EQ lets you sculpt that precisely.
eq.tip: EQ is mostly subtractive in professional practice — cut what you don't need rather than boosting everything. Boosting adds energy; cutting cleans up the mix. In Intermediate the Equalizer has three knobs like a simple mixing desk: Low and High are shelves, Mid is a bell. "Parametric" means you set each band's frequency and width yourself — that is what the Parametric Equalizer in Advanced adds, with a curve you can drag and a Bell / Shelf choice for Low and High. Feed it a stereo wire and both sides get the same settings.

graphic-eq.what: The Graphic EQ divides the spectrum into fixed frequency bands (here: 31 bands, three per octave — a third of an octave each — from 20 Hz to 20 kHz). Each band has its own fader — push it up to boost that band, pull it down to cut. The line across the sliders shows the shape you have drawn. Wire it to the L or R of a bus or its Main Fader (or feed it any stereo wire) and it works on both sides: the whole mix comes in on one wire and leaves as L and R, ready for an amplifier or two speakers. The sliders then split in two — Left on top, Right below — so each side can be shaped on its own; the right side starts as a copy of the left. Fed one channel, it stays single-channel.
graphic-eq.why: Graphic EQs are found on the master output of PA systems as the final tool for correcting room acoustics — a sudden peak at 4 kHz, a resonant boom at 63 Hz. They are less precise than parametric EQs but faster to use for broad shaping.
graphic-eq.tip: In live sound the graphic EQ on the master output is used mainly to prevent feedback and correct for the room, not to shape the mix. Keep moves gentle — small cuts (−3 to −6 dB) solve most problems. Large boosts cause feedback and distortion.

comp.what: The compressor reduces the dynamic range of the signal — it automatically turns down loud peaks and can be used with makeup gain to raise the overall level. It makes quiet parts relatively louder and loud parts relatively quieter.
comp.why: Live performances and recordings have wide dynamic ranges. Without compression, loud notes clip and quiet notes get lost. Compression makes the signal more consistent and controlled.
comp.tip: Watch the gain reduction meter. 2-6 dB of gain reduction is transparent and musical. More than 10 dB starts to sound pumped and squashed — which can be an effect in itself. When a stereo wire comes in, both sides are turned down together (linked) — the louder side decides — so the sound does not drift left or right.

fader.what: The channel fader controls the volume of this signal as it enters the mix. Unity gain (0 dB) means the signal passes through unchanged. Moving it down attenuates the signal.
fader.why: Every instrument in a mix needs to sit at the right level relative to everything else. The fader is how you set that balance. It is the primary mixing control.
fader.tip: In a mix, most faders end up below unity. The art of mixing is in the relative balance between all channels, not in making each one as loud as possible. Fed a stereo wire, one fader moves both sides together.

main-fader.what: A fader wired straight after a bus becomes its Main Fader. It controls the whole mix with one handle — left and right move together — and the bus's L and R outputs move onto it, so the speakers now hang off the fader. Its Matrix send moves too, so Matrix Buses always get the mix after this fader.
main-fader.why: This is the last level control before the speakers: it turns the whole mix up or down without changing the balance you built on the channels. One handle means left and right can never drift apart.
main-fader.tip: Take a second wire from the bus's Mix output: it does not change when you move this fader, because it leaves before the fader. That is where a pre-fade listen (PFL) path starts. Effects such as a limiter may sit between the bus and this fader — it stays the Main Fader.

amp.what: A power amplifier takes a line-level signal and boosts it to speaker-driving level — adding significant current, not just voltage. A passive speaker (one without a built-in amp) requires a power amplifier to produce any sound. Its Volume knob only turns down: at 0 dB (fully up) the signal goes on unchanged, which is already plenty for the speaker. Turning it up further would only make a good line-level signal clip. Wire it to the L or R of a bus, its Main Fader or a Graphic EQ (or feed it any stereo wire) and it becomes a two-channel amp: the whole mix comes in on one wire, each side gets its own Volume knob and its own output, L and R — one per speaker. Fed one channel, it stays a single-channel amp.
amp.why: Line-level signals are powerful enough for mixing and processing, but not powerful enough to physically move a speaker cone. The power amp provides the current needed to do the work.
amp.tip: Power amps are rated in watts. For studio monitors you typically need 50–100 W. For live PA systems, 500–2000 W per side is common. More wattage = more headroom before clipping, not necessarily more loudness.

switch.what: A switch (or mute button) is the simplest control in a signal chain. When it is on, the signal passes through unchanged. When it is off, the signal is completely cut — silence.
switch.why: Muting is used to silence a channel between takes, to prevent feedback when a microphone is not in use, or to isolate a track during a mix.
switch.tip: In live sound, muting microphones when not in use prevents bleed, handling noise, and feedback. It is a habit every sound engineer develops quickly.

aux-bus.what: An aux bus collects several signals and adds them together. Its one input takes as many wires as you like. In Mono everything leaves on one wire. Switch it to Stereo to keep left and right apart: the mix then leaves on two wires, L and R. In Stereo, a Fader wired to L or R becomes its Main Fader, just like on the Master Bus.
aux-bus.why: Use it to group sources that belong together — all backing vocals, all drums — so one control sets their combined level, or to send a separate mix to a monitor or an effect.
aux-bus.tip: Try this: set a Line Input to Stereo and wire it into a Mono aux bus. Left and right are added together and the level jumps by about 6 dB. That is why a stereo mix can suddenly get louder (or clip) when it is folded down to mono.

matrix-bus.what: A matrix bus is a mix of your mixes. Only finished mixes go in, after their fader — the Master Bus or an Aux Bus — never a single microphone or instrument. Wire a bus's L or R output into the matrix and the wire becomes its Matrix send: one stereo wire that carries left and right together, drawn as a twin line in its own colour and marked L+R. A mono Aux Bus goes in from its output, or from the Fader after it, and lands on both sides at the same level. Each bus gets one knob on the card that sets how much of it goes in. A matrix bus is always stereo: its mix leaves on two wires, L and R.
matrix-bus.why: Different places need a different blend, and the main mix must not change for them: small speakers along the front edge of the stage that need more vocals, delay speakers at the back of a hall, a speaker in the lobby, a feed for a recording or a livestream. Put a Fader after it to set its overall level — that Fader becomes its Main Fader.
matrix-bus.tip: Try this: give the Master Bus a Main Fader, then wire the fader's L output into the matrix. Move the Main Fader: the matrix follows, because the send leaves after the fader — that is how matrix sends work on a real mixing desk. Try a microphone too: the matrix input does not light up, because a microphone is not a mix.

balance.what: A balance control adjusts the relative loudness between the Left and Right channels of a stereo signal. At centre, both channels pass through equally. Turning left fades out the right channel; turning right fades out the left channel.
balance.why: Useful when a stereo source sounds off-centre — for example, a recording where the guitarist is too far left — nudge the balance to compensate without re-mixing the source.
balance.tip: Balance is what the Pan card becomes when you feed it a stereo wire. At centre both sides pass at full level — no −3 dB like a pan knob. Turning it left only fades the right side; the left side never gets louder. Keep it near centre unless a stereo source really sounds off-centre.

master-bus.what: The master bus is the final mixing point where every channel is added together before the sound leaves the system. Its one input takes as many wires as you like; the mix leaves on two wires, L and R — one for each speaker. A stereo wire keeps its left and right. A wire from another bus's L or R output stays on its side. A mono wire lands on both sides at full level — put a Pan knob in front to place it. Wire a Fader to its L or R output and it becomes the Main Fader: the L and R outputs move onto the fader.
master-bus.why: The master bus controls the overall output level. It is also the place for final mix bus processing — subtle compression or limiting to control peaks and add cohesion.
master-bus.tip: Leave headroom on the master bus — keep it in the green, at or below 0 dBu (unity). Above that it turns yellow (hot): there is less room left before it clips at +20 dBu, and a limiter or the next device has less to work with.

speaker.what: A passive speaker converts electrical signal back into sound, but it has no built-in amplifier. It needs a separate power amplifier (Amp node) to drive it — connecting one directly to line level will produce no sound.
speaker.why: Passive speakers are the standard in live sound PA systems and hi-fi setups. The amplifier is a separate unit chosen for its power output and impedance matching to the speaker.
speaker.tip: Connect an Amp node before this speaker. The amplifier provides the current needed to physically move the speaker cone. Without it, the signal is there but nothing moves.

active-speaker.what: An active (powered) speaker has a built-in amplifier. It accepts line-level signals directly from a mixer, audio interface, or any line-level output — no separate power amp needed.
active-speaker.why: Active speakers are the standard in modern studio monitors and portable PA setups. The built-in amplifier is matched to the speaker driver, which is why powered monitors tend to have more consistent, accurate sound.
active-speaker.tip: The volume knob adjusts the final output level. Good gain staging means getting a healthy green signal to this speaker — then use the volume knob to set how loud you want to listen, not to compensate for a too-quiet or too-loud chain. Never plug it into an Amplifier's output: that signal is already strong enough to drive a passive speaker, far too much for the line input of a speaker with its own amp inside — it blows.

di-box.what: A DI box (Direct Injection) converts a high-impedance unbalanced instrument signal — like a guitar or keyboard — into a low-impedance balanced signal that travels cleanly over long cables to a mixing desk. It has two outputs: an XLR output (balanced, for the preamp) and a Direct Output (instrument-level thru, for connecting to an amplifier at the same time).
di-box.why: Guitar pickups and keyboards have a high output impedance. Running them directly into a mixer causes high-frequency tone loss and picks up interference over long cables. The DI box solves both: it presents the correct high-impedance load to the instrument and converts the signal to a noise-resistant balanced format.
di-box.tip: The Ground Lift switch disconnects the cable screen at the DI box end, which breaks ground loops — a common cause of low-frequency hum. If you hear a 50 or 60 Hz buzz, try switching ground lift on.

noise-gate.what: A noise gate is a switch controlled by level. When the signal rises above the threshold, the gate opens and the signal passes through unchanged. When the signal falls below the threshold, the gate closes and the output is silence.
noise-gate.why: Every microphone and cable picks up some background noise — air conditioning hum, electrical interference, room ambience. Between musical phrases, when the performer is quiet, that noise is audible. The gate simply closes during those quiet moments, removing the noise before it reaches the mix.
noise-gate.tip: Set the threshold just above the noise floor and just below the quietest musical content. Too high, and the gate clips the start of notes (chatter). Too low, and the noise gets through. The OPEN/CLOSED indicator shows you exactly when the gate fires. Range is how far it turns down when closed: all the way (−80 dB, silence) or only a little, so the background drops without vanishing. Attack is how fast it opens, Hold keeps it open for a moment after the sound stops, and Release is how gently it closes.

limiter.what: A limiter is a compressor with an extremely high ratio — effectively infinite. It sets a hard ceiling: no signal can exceed the threshold, no matter how loud the input gets. Below the ceiling, the signal passes through unchanged.
limiter.why: Limiters protect equipment and listeners from sudden loud peaks. A drum hit, a mic bump, a loud vocal phrase — without limiting, any of these can clip the mix bus, damage amplifiers, or cause hearing damage at high volumes. The limiter is the safety net at the end of the chain.
limiter.tip: Unlike a compressor, a limiter is meant to be invisible — you should not hear it working. If you see the 'Limiting' indicator light up often, the signal going into the limiter is too hot. Fix it earlier in the chain rather than relying on the limiter to tame a consistently loud signal.

pad.what: A pad is a fixed attenuator — a passive circuit that drops the signal level by a set amount, usually 20 dB. It sits inline in the signal path. When the pad is engaged (button shows −20 dB), the signal is reduced by 20 dB. When disengaged, the signal passes through unchanged.
pad.why: Microphones in front of loud sources — kick drums, guitar amps, brass instruments — can produce a signal so strong that even the preamp at its lowest gain setting is too loud. The pad solves this by cutting the level before it even reaches the preamp's gain stage, preventing distortion at the input.
pad.tip: Engage the pad before you record if your input meter is clipping even with the gain turned all the way down. The 20 dB drop is a lot — if the signal then becomes too quiet, raise the preamp gain to compensate and find the right balance.

deesser.what: A de-esser is a frequency-selective compressor. It listens for harsh sibilance — the sharp hissing sounds of letters like 'S', 'SH', and 'CH' in vocal recordings — and automatically reduces only those frequencies when they get too loud. You set the frequency and threshold; the de-esser does the rest automatically.
deesser.why: Microphones and certain processing (especially EQ boosts in the 5–10 kHz range) can exaggerate sibilance until it becomes painful to listen to. A broadband compressor would make everything quieter, which is not the goal. The de-esser targets only the problem frequencies, leaving the rest of the voice untouched.
deesser.tip: Set the frequency to where the sibilance is worst — usually 5–8 kHz for most voices, sometimes up to 10 kHz for brighter voices. The gain reduction meter shows how much de-essing is happening. A little (1–3 dB) is transparent. Heavy de-essing (6+ dB) can make voices sound lispy.

relay.what: A relay is an electronic switch that routes your signal to one of two outputs. You choose Output A or Output B — the chosen path gets the signal; the other carries nothing. This is used for A/B routing: for example, sending a guitar to an amp (A) or directly to the interface (B) without unplugging cables.
relay.why: In live sound and recording, you often need to switch between two signal paths instantly — different monitor mixes, parallel processing chains, or backup routes. A relay does this cleanly without noise or clicks.
relay.tip: The active output is highlighted in green; the inactive one is grey. Try connecting Output A to a reverb bus and Output B to a dry speaker to instantly switch between wet and dry monitoring.

pan.what: Feed it a mono signal and this is a Pan knob: it spreads that one signal between Left and Right and sends both out on one stereo wire. Fully left, only the left side gets it; fully right, only the right side. At centre each side gets it 3 dB quieter, so the overall loudness stays the same. Feed it a stereo wire and it turns into a Balance knob on its own.
pan.why: A mono signal — one microphone, one guitar — has no left or right of its own. Wired straight into a stereo bus it lands on both sides at full level: stuck in the middle and 3 dB louder than a centred pan. The Pan knob is how you place it anywhere between the speakers.
pan.tip: Compare: Line Input → Pan at centre → the Master shows 3 dB less on each side than the same Line Input wired straight into the Master. Then set the Line Input to Stereo: the card turns into Balance. A balance knob does not spread one signal, it only turns down one side of a signal that already has two.

adc.what: An Analog-to-Digital Converter (ADC) samples the continuously varying analog voltage from your gear thousands of times per second and converts each measurement into a digital number. The level scale changes from dBu (analog) to dBFS (digital full scale). With the standard alignment, 0 dBu (unity) becomes −18 dBFS — so the digital ceiling, 0 dBFS, is +18 dBu. Healthy analog levels land well below it.
adc.why: Computers work with numbers, not voltages. The ADC is the bridge between the physical world of microphones and amplifiers and the digital world of DAWs and plugins. Everything after the ADC is math, not electricity.
adc.tip: 0 dBFS is the ceiling in digital audio — there is no louder. Unlike analog gear which can go a few dB over nominal before distorting, digital clips instantly and harshly at 0 dBFS. Aim to keep peaks well below 0 dBFS (−18 to −6 dBFS) to protect against sudden transients.

dac.what: A Digital-to-Analog Converter (DAC) does the reverse of an ADC: it reads the digital numbers from your computer and reconstructs a continuously varying analog voltage. Using the same alignment, −18 dBFS becomes 0 dBu (unity) again, and anything after the DAC is back in the analog world.
dac.why: Speakers and amplifiers are analog devices — they respond to voltage, not numbers. The DAC converts the digital mix back into real electrical signal so you can hear it through speakers. Without a DAC, digital audio stays in the computer.
dac.tip: Place the DAC before any analog gear that follows — amplifiers, passive speakers, analog signal processors. The domain indicator on the node turns green (analog) after the DAC, confirming that everything downstream is back in the correct electrical domain.
